prize_parts.citation: For a poetic oeuvre that has renewed the language and forms of Arabic poetry through myth, fragmentation and a critical dialogue with its own inherited tradition, with an essayistic companion body of work.

statement.case_for: My laureate is unchanged: Adonis, B002. The change is in the citation, which I have narrowed in response to the chair's scoping question. It now names the poetry as the credited achievement and mentions the essays only as a companion strand. The claim is a formal and linguistic one. Public knowledge, as summarised in the entry, points to a decades-long project that recast Arabic poetic language by setting myth, fragmentation and prose-poem forms against the classical inheritance. The representative works are Songs of Mihyar the Damascene and A Time Between Ashes and Roses. On the common criteria, distinctiveness of voice and formal and linguistic achievement carry the case. Imaginative and intellectual depth is supported by the essays on tradition and change as a counterpart to the verse. The oeuvre is long and fully formed, so maturity here concerns whether quality was sustained, not whether the work developed. I treat the Cărtărescu case as serious and strong. The round-1 exchange has not given me a reason to think the claim to have changed what the poem can do in a whole literary language is weaker than the claim to have built a single large prose cosmos. I do not rest the case on the writer's age, public standing or political position.
statement.case_against: The core of the claim lies in prosody, sound and intertextual play in Arabic, which I cannot assess directly and which reaches me only partly through translation. My case therefore rests on reception and description more heavily than a prose case does. I should say so plainly: the committee can verify Cărtărescu's achievement of architecture somewhat better than it can verify Adonis's achievement of prosody. I also cannot establish the quality and consistency of the later collections, or how much weight the essays should carry beside the poems. If colleagues who can read Arabic, or the translators' testimony, cannot show that the verse sustains its quality across decades, the claim for B012 becomes the one that can be better stated and defended. That is the condition under which I would move.

responses.point: Olsson, the chair, prefers Cărtărescu and holds Adonis as his strongest alternative. He argues that translation risk is roughly symmetrical between the two, because Arabic prosody cannot be tested through translation while Cărtărescu's architecture and scale reach us at least partly.
responses.response: I take the chair's distinction between what is testable and what is not, and I concede part of it: architecture and structure survive translation better than prosody does. Where I differ is on what follows. The risk is asymmetric, but a claim that is harder to verify is not thereby a lesser achievement. I would answer the chair's evidence question this way. The committee could rely on the consistency of the poetry across decades as shown in the translated collections, the quality and number of independent translations, and the poets' and critics' reception within Arabic. It should then draft the citation to claim only form, voice and renewal of poetic language, and make no claim about sound or metre. I agree with him that the citation should name the poetry. I have now narrowed my wording accordingly.

responses.point: Palm prefers Cărtărescu and ranks Adonis second. She finds the sustained architecture across several large works a somewhat stronger demonstration of sustained quality than she can establish for poetry through translation. She also says the limit is on her judgment, not a mark against him.
responses.response: Palm separates her inability to verify the prosody from any verdict on Adonis, and I think that distinction is honest and important. I agree that the sustained-quality criterion is easier to show across several large prose works. My reply is that a decades-long poetic project in one language can show sustained quality too, if the collections remain distinctive across time. That is exactly what I cannot confirm for the later work, and I do not wish to overstate it. Her own caution that Cărtărescu's scale could be admired over finished execution is a point where our uncertainties meet. Neither of us can settle it from translation.

responses.point: Mattson prefers Cărtărescu. She says she would need colleagues who read Arabic to speak to how much of the Adonis claim is the poems and how much the essayistic and historical role. She tests Cărtărescu by whether the late novel does something the earlier trilogy did not.
responses.response: I accept her challenge. Nobody on the committee has been identified as a reader of Arabic, and I will not claim that expertise. That is a real gap, and it is why I narrowed the citation to the poetry. On the question of poems versus essays, my position is that the poems carry the credit and the essays are context for them. I find her test for Cărtărescu, whether the late novel does something new, a fair and precise one, and I would apply the same test to Adonis. I cannot show it for the late collections from the supplied evidence, and I would not hide that. It remains an open weakness in my case.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg prefers Cărtărescu. He argues that the formal control over very large structures is a more fully legible achievement for a committee that cannot read the Arabic. He would test whether a citation can be justified from specific works, and not from reputation for size.
responses.response: His test of justifying the citation from specific works is the right one, and I apply it to myself. For Adonis, the works the case can name with some confidence are Songs of Mihyar the Damascene and A Time Between Ashes and Roses, so the citation should rest on those and on the formal renewal they represent. I agree that legibility counts for something in a recommendation. I do not think legibility alone should outweigh the scale of what a poet changed in a language. I would rather the committee state the limits of the Adonis case openly than turn those limits into a reason against it.

responses.point: Carlberg also prefers Adonis. She would anchor the citation in the poetry with the essays as a companion, keep political positioning out of it, and accepts that the Cărtărescu case is more directly testable from translations.
responses.response: I agree with her scoping and have used it. We share one risk that I want to be candid about. Two members who prefer Adonis are leaning on the same limited reception of poetry in translation, so our agreement does not add independent evidence. I do not count it as such. I also agree that the Cărtărescu case is easier to test, and that is the strongest consideration against my own preference.

uncertainties: How much of the formal and prosodic innovation in Adonis's poetry reaches readers in translation, and whether the translated editions are adequate witnesses for a committee that has no identified Arabic reader among its members.
The quality and consistency of the later collections, which I cannot verify from the supplied evidence.
The relative weight of the essays against the poetry, and whether even a companion mention in the citation pulls the award toward critical writing.
Whether Cărtărescu's late large-scale work develops beyond elaboration of a single mode, and how much of his prose texture is lost in translation. This bears on my first alternative.
Whether the translation asymmetry I describe is a real difference in verifiability or partly an effect of my own limited coverage.
I have not read or independently verified any of the works. I rely on the entry, public reputation and colleagues' round-1 statements, and I make no claim about confidential proceedings.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile, which records no personal or institutional tie to any shortlisted writer. My own literary practice (family drama, love and obsession, WWII-era refugee fiction) is context only, not evidence of preference. My 2021 public remarks about overlooked women's authorships are attributed statements, and I do not use gender or any similar consideration as a criterion of literary merit in this configuration.
